notes.669: 676: 'funestam' does not agree with 'penetrale'; taken as funestum. 691: the punctuation after 'telum est' is odd; 'what the deepest earth creates' is taken with the cheap weapon. Line 711 stands before 710 in the text as given and is translated in that order. 710: 'Mediis' does not construe with 'pugnax'; taken as Medus, 'the Mede'. 715: 'discnssit' read as discussit. 740: 'Compreeor' read as comprecor.
notes.815: 815: the sentence begins before the unit ('the reason for calling on your ... bow so often'). 820: 'elusus' ('tricked, cheated') is doubtful; perhaps for inclusus, 'shut in'. 837: 'meet' read as meat, 'let pass'. 838: 'tument', 'swell', is indicative among wishes and may be a slip for fument, 'smoke'.

nodes.text: spare him who was commanded.
Nurse
My mind trembles, it shudders: a great disaster is at hand.
It is monstrous how her pain grows, and kindles
itself by itself, and renews its former force.
I have often seen her raging and assailing the gods,
drawing down the sky: greater than these, greater
is the horror Medea prepares. For as soon as with frenzied step
she went out and reached her deadly inner shrine,
she pours out all her resources, and whatever for a long time
even she herself has feared she brings out, and unfolds the whole
crowd of evils, things arcane, secret, hidden;
and, gathering the grim rite with her left hand,
she calls up the plagues, whatever the burning
sand of Libya breeds, and those that with everlasting snow
the Taurus holds fast, stiff with Arctic cold,
and every monster. Drawn by magic chants,
the scaly crowd is here from its deserted lairs.
Here a savage serpent drags its immense body
and darts out its three-forked tongue and looks for those to whom
it may come bringing death; hearing the spell it is stunned,
and folds its body, swollen with heaped-up coils,
and forces it into rings. 'Small are these evils,' she says,
'and cheap the weapon, what the deepest earth creates:
I shall seek poisons from the sky. Now, now is the time
to set in motion something higher than common trickery.
Let that one, sprawling like a vast torrent, come
down here, the serpent whose immense coils the two
beasts, the greater and the lesser, feel
(the greater a guide for the Pelasgians, the lesser for the Sidonians);
and let Ophiuchus at last loosen his gripping hands
and pour out the venom; let there come to my chants
Python, who dared to provoke the twin deities;
and let the Hydra return, and every serpent cut down by the hand
of Hercules, restoring itself by its own slaughter.
You too, ever-wakeful one, leave Colchis behind and come,
you, serpent, first lulled to sleep by my chants.'
When she has called forth every kind of serpent,
she heaps together the evil things of ill-omened growth:
whatever Eryx, pathless with its rocks, produces;
what is borne, on ridges covered by everlasting winter,
by Caucasus, spattered with the blood of Prometheus;
and those with which the rich Arabs smear their arrows
and the Mede, warlike with his quiver, or the light Parthians;
or the juices which, under the cold sky, are gathered
by the noble Suebian women in the Hyrcanian groves;
whatever the earth creates in the nest-building spring,
or when stiff winter has already shaken down the glory
of the woods and bound all things fast with snowy frost;
whatever plant flourishes with deadly flower,
or whose strong juice in its roots
breeds the means of harm: she handles it with her hand.
Haemonian Athos contributed those plagues,
huge Pindus these; that one, on the ridges of Pangaeus,
laid down its tender foliage to a bloody sickle;
these the Tigris nourished, pressing down its deep flood,
the Danube those; these, through parched regions,
the gem-bearing Hydaspes, running with warm waters,
and the Baetis, which gave its name to its own lands,
beating the Hesperian seas with languid stream.
This one suffered the blade while Phoebus prepares the day;
that one's stem was cut in the depth of night;
but this one's crop was cut with an enchanted fingernail.
She plucks deadly grasses, and of serpents
squeezes out the gore, and mixes in foul birds,
and the heart of the mournful horned owl, and of the hoarse screech-owl
the innards, cut out alive. These the craftswoman of crimes
sets out separately: in these is the ravening force of fire,
in these the icy chill of sluggish frost.
To the poisons she adds words no less
to be feared than they. Look, her frenzied step has sounded,
and she sings. The world trembles at her first words.
Medea
I pray to the throng of the silent, and to you, gods of the dead,
bow so often is one and the same:
always Jason.
Now dye Creusa's robes,
so that, as soon as she has put them on, deep in her
marrow a creeping flame may burn.
Fire, hidden by a trick in the tawny gold,
lies dark; it was given to me by him who for the thefts
of heaven pays with his teeming liver;
he gave it, and taught me to store up its powers
by art, Prometheus; and Mulciber gave
fires concealed in thin sulphur,
and bolts of living flame
I took from my kinsman Phaethon.
See, I have the gifts of the dread Chimaera,
I have flames
snatched from the scorched throat of the bull,
which, with Medusa's gall mixed in,
I have ordered to keep their evil silent.
Add goads to the poisons, Hecate,
and in my gifts
keep stored the seeds of flame.
Let them deceive the sight and endure the touch;
let the heat pass into her breast and veins;
let her limbs drip, her bones swell,
and may she outdo her own
torches with her blazing hair, the new bride.
My prayers are granted: three barks
has bold Hecate given, and sacred
fires she has sent forth from her light-bringing torch.
All the power is accomplished: call the sons here,
through whom I may carry precious gifts to the bride.
